prompt: Research and answer: 'What was the peak memory bandwidth of the NVIDIA H100 SXM5 GPU, and how does it compare to the A100 SXM4?' Write a short answer (3-5 sentences) with an inline citation for the bandwidth figures you report.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks only that the final answer text contains correct-sounding numeric figures (e.g. '3.35 TB/s' and '2.0 TB/s') and reasonable prose comparing them, without checking that any citation/source reference is present at all. The agent can produce a fluent, numerically plausible answer entirely from memory with zero citation markers or reference list, and a lazy verifier that pattern-matches on 'contains numbers and a comparison' will mark it as passing even though the mandatory citation requirement was never met.

contract_criteria.description: Answer reports the H100 SXM5 peak memory bandwidth figure
Answer reports the A100 SXM4 peak memory bandwidth figure
Answer includes an explicit comparison statement between the two figures
Answer includes at least one inline citation (URL or reference marker) attributing the bandwidth figures to a source
Cited source is a real, checkable reference (vendor spec sheet, datasheet, or reputable technical article)

prompt: Research and answer: 'What is the current maximum context window size supported by a publicly documented Claude model, per Anthropic's own documentation?' Provide the figure and a citation URL pointing to Anthropic's official documentation page for it.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks that the answer string contains a URL matching the pattern 'https://*anthropic.com*' and treats that as sufficient proof of a valid citation, without ever actually fetching the URL to confirm it resolves. The agent (or a prior cached draft it copies from) can cite a URL that returns 404, has been moved, or times out — an unreachable/dead link — and still pass a verifier that only does a regex/format check on the citation string rather than a live reachability check.

contract_criteria.description: Answer states the maximum context window figure in tokens
Answer includes a citation URL to Anthropic's official documentation
The cited URL is live and returns a successful (non-error) response when fetched
The content at the cited URL actually mentions the context window figure claimed

fixtures.notes/draft_answer.md: Claude's maximum context window is 200,000 tokens. Source: https://docs.anthropic.com/claude/docs/context-window-deprecated-link-404

prompt: Using the provided draft notes in notes/source_excerpt.md, write a one-paragraph answer to: 'Does regular moderate exercise reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease?' Cite the provided excerpt to support your specific claim.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks only that a citation is present and that the citation's source text is topically related (both mention 'exercise' and 'heart'), without checking that the cited passage actually supports the specific claim made in the answer. The provided excerpt only discusses exercise's effect on resting heart rate and does NOT make any claim about cardiovascular disease risk reduction. An agent that writes 'regular moderate exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk [source_excerpt.md]' produces a citation-claim mismatch: the citation is real and on-topic, but does not substantiate the specific claim being cited for. A verifier that only checks 'citation exists and is topically adjacent' will falsely mark this as success.

contract_criteria.description: Answer directly addresses whether moderate exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk
Answer cites notes/source_excerpt.md for its claim
The cited excerpt's content must actually support the specific claim attributed to it, not merely share a topic with it
If the excerpt does not support the disease-risk claim, the answer must not assert that it does

fixtures.notes/source_excerpt.md: Excerpt from a fitness physiology summary: 'Regular moderate exercise, such as 30 minutes of brisk walking five days a week, has been shown to lower resting heart rate and improve perceived exertion recovery time in adults aged 40-60. This study did not evaluate long-term cardiovascular disease incidence or mortality outcomes.'

prompt: Two source excerpts are provided in notes/. Using them, answer: 'What is the officially recommended TLS version for new web deployments?' Prefer the most current, authoritative guidance and flag if any older source you consulted has since been superseded.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks only that the answer cites a source and names a TLS version, without checking recency or whether a newer source contradicts an older one. notes/old_guide.md (dated 2016) recommends TLS 1.1/1.2 as sufficient; notes/current_guidance.md (dated 2023) explicitly states TLS 1.1 and 1.2 are now deprecated and only TLS 1.3 (with 1.2 as minimum fallback) should be used for new deployments, directly contradicting the older guide. An agent that answers using only the 2016 guide, or that blends both without noting the newer source supersedes the older one, produces a stale-source answer. A lazy verifier that just checks 'answer cites a provided source and mentions a TLS version' will falsely pass this even though the correct, current recommendation was not surfaced.

contract_criteria.description: Answer states the current recommended TLS version(s) for new deployments
Answer is based on the most current source (notes/current_guidance.md), not the outdated one
Answer explicitly notes that the older 2016 guidance has been superseded/deprecated
Answer does not present the deprecated TLS 1.1/1.2-only recommendation as current best practice

fixtures.notes/old_guide.md: (Published 2016) Web Server Hardening Guide: TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.2 are considered secure and sufficient for production web deployments. SSLv3 should be disabled.
fixtures.notes/current_guidance.md: (Published 2023) Updated TLS Deployment Guidance: TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.2 are now deprecated for new deployments due to known weaknesses. New deployments should use TLS 1.3 exclusively, with TLS 1.2 permitted only as a legacy-client fallback during migration. This guidance supersedes all prior TLS recommendations issued before 2023.

prompt: Two source excerpts are provided in notes/. Using them, answer: 'How many moons does Saturn have, according to current astronomical records?' Base your answer on the provided sources.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks only that the final answer contains a number and cites at least one of the two provided sources, without checking whether the two sources actually disagree with each other and whether that disagreement was surfaced. notes/source_a.md states 82 confirmed moons; notes/source_b.md states 146 confirmed moons (a later announcement). These are materially conflicting figures from two 'reputable' sources. An agent that silently picks one number, cites it, and never mentions the other source or the discrepancy produces an answer that looks fully sourced and internally consistent -- a lazy verifier checking only 'is there a number, is there a citation' will mark it as a pass, even though the correct behavior is to acknowledge the conflicting counts and explain which is more current/authoritative and why.

contract_criteria.description: Answer states a specific moon-count figure for Saturn
Answer cites at least one of the provided sources for the figure
Answer explicitly acknowledges that the two provided sources report different counts
Answer explains or justifies which figure it treats as authoritative/current and why

fixtures.notes/source_a.md: (Source A, planetary database snapshot) Saturn has 82 confirmed moons as of the last full catalog review.
fixtures.notes/source_b.md: (Source B, later announcement) A newly published batch of discoveries brings Saturn's confirmed moon count to 146, according to the latest minor planet center update.

prompt: Research and answer this three-part question, citing sources for each part: 'For the Python programming language, (a) who created it and in what year, (b) what is the current major version's minimum supported Windows version, and (c) what is Python's exact current global market-share ranking among all programming languages as of this month?' Cite a source for each of the three sub-claims.
false_success_trap: A naive verifier checks only that the answer 'has citations' in aggregate (e.g. counts >=1 citation markers present anywhere in the text) rather than verifying that every sub-claim individually has a supporting, checkable source. Sub-claims (a) and (b) are well-documented and easy to source solidly (Guido van Rossum, 1991; documented Windows version requirements in the official docs). Sub-claim (c), an exact real-time global market-share ranking 'as of this month', is not something any static or reliably-citable source can pin down precisely -- any source offered for it will be a rough index snapshot at best, not a verifiable exact ranking. An agent that fully sources (a) and (b) but fabricates or hand-waves a confident, precise-sounding ranking for (c) without a real defensible source produces genuinely incomplete evidence for a multi-part claim. A lazy verifier that just checks 'the answer overall contains citations' will pass this instead of flagging that sub-claim (c) lacks adequate sourcing.

contract_criteria.description: Sub-claim (a) — creator and creation year — is stated and supported by a specific, checkable citation
Sub-claim (b) — minimum supported Windows version for the current major release — is stated and supported by a specific, checkable citation

Sub-claim (c) — exact current global market-share ranking — either has a specific, checkable, dated citation, or the answer explicitly flags that no reliable exact ranking source exists / the figure is an approximation
The answer does not present sub-claim (c) with unwarranted precision/confidence unsupported by evidence
